3. In order to establish guilt of the accused Ajay Kumar, prosecution has examined nine witnesses in all.
After prosecution evidence, statement of accused Ajay u/s 313 Cr.P.C. was recorded wherein all the incriminating circumstances were put to accused.
The accused did not opt to lead evidence in his defence.
Final arguments were heard.
4. I have heard the rival contentions advanced on behalf of the prosecution and defence and have also gone through the case file carefully.
State Vs.: Rakesh Kumar Yadav FIR No: 453/2005 U/s 420/34 IPC P.S.Vikas Puri 4 5.

The allegations leveled against the accused are that the accused Ajay along with his co-accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead) in furtherance of common intention of each other cheated complainant Seema Bajaj by dishonestly inducing her to deliver Rs. 1,09,500/-, out of which Rs.6000/- were received by accused Ajay Kumar and Rs.1,03,500/- were received by accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead) on the pretext and with the assurance of delivering her three second hand vehicles.

The allegations are also to the extent that the accused persons also gave a receipt to the complainant at the time of receiving the money but they failed to deliver the vehicles to the complainant and even to return the amount so received by them and thereby constituting offences u/s 420/34 IPC.
6.

It has been contended by Ld. APP for the State that the prosecution has established beyond all reasonable doubts that accused Ajay Kumar has dishonestly induced the complainant to part with money on the pretext of delivering them the second hand vehicles but neither the vehicles were delivered to the complainant nor the money paid by her was returned and thereby has committed offences punishable u/s 420/34 IPC.
Ld. APP for State further submits that the accused deserves to be convicted for the alleged offence.
7. Per contra, Ld. Defence Counsel has argued that the accused has been falsely implicated in the present case.

It has also been argued that the prosecution has failed to establish any nexus State Vs.:
Rakesh Kumar Yadav FIR No: 453/2005 U/s 420/34 IPC P.S.Vikas Puri 5 between the accused Ajay Kumar and co-accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead).

It has also been argued that the delivery of the alleged amount of Rs. 6,000/- in favour of accused Ajay Kumar by the complainant has not been established by the prosecution through any reliable evidences and that even the alleged cheques issued in favour of complainant towards the repayment of the money paid by her were not issued by accused Ajay Kumar and rather same belongs to accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead), hence, the accused Ajay Kumar cannot be held liable for the alleged offence.

It has also been argued that there also lie material contradictions in the version of prosecution witnesses, hence,
accused deserves to be acquitted for the alleged offences.

10. This is the entire evidence on case record.
11. Having discussed the testimonies of prosecution witnesses, now let us advert ourselves to the merits of the present case.

12. The allegations against accused pertains to offence u/s 420/34 IPC.
13.
It is pertinent to mention that the accused Ajay has been indicted for the offence u/s 420/34 IPC with the aid of Section Section 34 IPC.

As the accused has been charged for the offence u/s 420 IPC with the aid of Section 34 IPC, hence it is necessary to delve into the discussion regarding the provisions of section 34 IPC and the evidences led by the prosecution in that regard.

Pertinently,
State Vs.: Rakesh Kumar Yadav FIR No: 453/2005 U/s 420/34 IPC P.S.Vikas Puri 12 Section 34 IPC also creates a principal of joint criminal liability and this provision is stricter than section 120B IPC.

To bring home the charge of common intention, prosecution has to establish by evidence, whether direct or circumstantial that there was plan or meeting of minds of all the accused persons to commit the offence for which they are charged with the aid of Section 34 IPC, be it a pre-arranged plan or plan made on the spur of moment but it must necessarily be formed before the commission State vs Rakesh Kumar Yadav on 9 April, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/145978822/
6 of crime.
Section 34 IPC does not lay down any distinct offence and rather it is a rule of evidence.
This provision also does not mandate actual commission of any overt act by any of the member of the party who has formulated the plan for committing an offence.

In the present case there is no evidence led by the prosecution to establish the existence of the common intention between accused Ajay Kumar and accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead), in furtherance of which they have allegedly cheated the complainant.

It is evident from the record that except the bald allegations to the extent the accused persons have entertained the prior criminal intention for cheating the complainant, there are no clinching evidences led by the prosecution in that regard.

More specifically, merely on the premise that the accused Ajay and co-accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead ) were related to each other as son and father respectively, it cannot be concluded that their acts were guided by the pre-arranged design to cheat the complainant.

The careful perusal of the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses would go on to reveal that there is nothing on record establishing that the accused Ajay Kumar along with his father/ co-accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav entered into prior concert or had formulated a pre- State Vs.: Rakesh Kumar Yadav FIR No: 453/2005 U/s 420/34 IPC P.S.Vikas Puri 13 arranged design for indulging into the act of cheating the complainant, hence in the considered view of this Court, the joint liability cannot be fastened upon the accused Ajay even with the aid of Section 34 IPC.
14 . Moving further, the other allegations against accused pertains to offences u/s 420 IPC.

So far as the allegations qua offence u/s 420 IPC are concerned, it is pertinent to state that the accused Ajay has been charge-sheeted for this offense on the premise that he in furtherance of common intention with his co-accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead) represented to the complainant that he was an authorized dealer of the banks for selling the repossessed bank vehicles and in pursuance of such representation, he induced the complainant for delivering Rs. 1,09,500/- towards the purchase of the three second hand vehicles in favour of the complainant but neither the vehicles were given to the complainant nor the amount received from her was returned by the accused.

15. The discussion made in the preceding part of the judgment clearly suggests that there is no iota of evidence on record to establish the common intention inter-se the accused persons, therefore, the accused Ajay cannot be held liable for the offence u/s 420 IPC with the aid of Section 34 IPC.

However, assumingly that there was a common intention entertained by the accused Ajay Kumar along with co-accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead) for committing such offences, then also,
the necessary ingredients for constituting such an offence have not been fulfilled in the present case.

It was incumbent upon the part of prosecution to State Vs.: Rakesh Kumar Yadav FIR No: 453/2005 U/s 420/34 IPC P.S.Vikas Puri 14 establish the following for successfully establishing the commission of offence u/s 420 IPC by the accused :-
a.)

16. The prosecution is primarily relying upon the testimony of PW-1, PW-2 and PW-7 for establishing its case.

The careful perusal of testimony of PW-1 would reflect that she was informed by the gate keeper / receptionist at Nanda Farm that accused Ajay Kumar and R. K. Yadav (since dead) were authorized by the banks for purchasing the repossessed vehicles which were selected by her.

Likewise, PW-2 has also narrated that upon his visit to Nanda Farms along with PW-1 and PW-7 the person at gate handed over the visiting card of accused Ajay Kumar in the name of R. K. & Company for purchasing the second-hand bank repossessed vehicles.

In a similar manner,
PW-7 has also narrated that when he along with PW-1 and PW-2 visited Nanda Farm House, a person State Vs.: Rakesh Kumar Yadav FIR No: 453/2005 U/s 420/34 IPC P.S.Vikas Puri 15 namely, Umesh Kumar who was working there provided the visiting card of accused persons for proceeding further with the purchase of the second-hand vehicles by the complainants.

From the above mentioned version of PW-1, PW-2 and PW-7, it is clear that no direct representation was made by the accused persons to the complainant that they were authorized by the banks concerned for selling the second hand vehicles and rather such facts were informed to the complainant by the gate keeper/receptionist/staff namely, Umesh Kumar who was present at the Nanda Farms.

The prosecution was duty bound to establish the fact that accused Ajay Kumar was not authorized by the banks concerned for selling the bank repossessed vehicles or that the representations made by the above-named Umesh Kumar to such extent were false.
However, there is no evidence to such extent on the entire case record.
Precisely, the prosecuting agency has failed to examine the afore- named Umesh Kumar as a witness in the present case.
The presence of the witness Umesh Kumar could not be secured by the prosecuting agency for the purpose of his further examination after 27.10.2023 as he remained untraceable.

The above-named witness Umesh Kumar was a crucial witness for establishing the fact that the representation made to the complainant qua the accused persons being authorized by the banks concerned for selling the second-hand vehicles was in fact a false representation but the said witness was never completely examined in the present case.
Besides, no efforts were made by the IOs for verifying the fact of authorization of the accused persons in dealing with the repossessed bank vehicles from the banks concerned.
No reasonable explanation for such crucial lapse has come from IOs State Vs.: Rakesh Kumar Yadav FIR No: 453/2005 U/s 420/34 IPC P.S.Vikas Puri 16 examined as PW-5 and PW-9.

The fact that accused Ajay Kumar was not authorized by the banks concerned for dealing with the resale of the second hand bank repossessed vehicles has not been proved by the prosecution by any convincing evidences, hence it cannot be held that the alleged State vs Rakesh Kumar Yadav on 9 April, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/145978822/
8 representation made by the accused to the complainant that he was authorized by the banks concerned for selling the second hand vehicles was a false representation, hence, the condition as mentioned at Point no. (a) above has not been established in the present case.

17. Further, as the discussion in the preceding part of the judgment suggests that the prosecution has not established the alleged representation made by the accused to the complainant that he was authorized by the banks concerned for selling the second-hand vehicles was the false representation,
hence due to such reasons, it cannot be held that the complainant was dishonestly induced by the accused for entering into the transaction qua the purchase of second hand vehicles for an amount of Rs. 1,09,500/-, hence the condition as mentioned at Point no. (b) above has also not been established in the present case.

18. Moving further, the careful perusal of the complaint dated 10.08.2005 Ex. PW 1/A would reflect that the complainant has narrated therein that out of the total amount of Rs. 1,09,500/-, payment of Rs. 1,03,500/- was made by her in favour of accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead) and remaining payment of Rs. 6000/- was made by her in favour of accused Ajay Kumar.

However,
during the course of his deposition, PW-1 has made considerable State Vs.: Rakesh Kumar Yadav FIR No: 453/2005 U/s 420/34 IPC P.S.Vikas Puri 17 improvements in her version qua making of the payment of the allegedly cheated amount in favour of accused persons.

More specifically, in contradiction with the version mentioned in the complaint Ex. PW 1/A, complainant has stated that apart from cash of Rs. 6000/-, she made payment of Rs. 23,800/- in favour of accused Ajay Kumar and such version of PW-1 has not been supported either by PW-2 or PW-7 in whose presence the alleged payments were made to the accused.

PW-2 during his deposition has stated that the amount which was settled for purchasing the vehicles was Rs. 1,04,000/- out of which Rs. 23,500/- were handed over the accused Ajay and subsequent payment of Rs. 80,000/- was made to accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead) as well as a further payment of Rs. 6000/- to accused Ajay.

PW-2 has even conceded to the fact that in the legal notice sent to the accused R. K. Yadav (since dead) the amount paid to the accused Ajay was mentioned as Rs. 5000/- and the remaining payments allegedly made to accused R. K. Yadav (since dead) were mentioned as Rs. 97,000/- which is apparently contradictory to the version narrated by him during his examination in chief.

Likewise,
in the testimony of PW-7 it has come that a bank draft of Rs. 6000/- was given by the complainant in favour of accused Ajay Kumar towards the part payment of the amount of Rs. 1,09,500/- for purchasing the second-hand vehicles, which is all together a new story which has only surfaced during the examination of PW-7.
The aforesaid demand draft has never seen the light of the day nor copy of the same was collected by the IO during the course of investigation.

Further, as per PW-1 when she along with PW-2 and PW-7 reached at Nanda Farm House, she first selected the three State Vs.: Rakesh Kumar Yadav FIR No: 453/2005 U/s 420/34 IPC P.S.Vikas Puri 18 vehicles intended to be purchased by her and thereafter, upon arrival of accused Ajay Kumar, he was informed about the vehicles so selected by her but such version of PW-1 is again in contradiction to the version narrated by PW-2 and PW-7 as both of them have narrated that the vehicles were shown to complainant by accused persons only after they arrived at Nanda Farms.
The prosecution has not explained the above-mentioned material contradictions which have surfaced in the testimony of the afore- named witnesses.
The payment of Rs. 6000/- stated to be made by the complainant in favour of accused Ajay Kumar has also not been proved through any reliable evidences.

9 PW-6 and PW-8 goes on to reveal that even the alleged cheques of Rs. One lac and Rs. 9500/-
respectively, pertained to bank account of accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead) and said bank account was in the name of accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav and Rama Yadav.

The accused Ajay Kumar has never issued the cheques in favour of the complainant for the repayment of the allegedly cheated amount nor the bank account to which said cheques pertained belonged to accused Ajay Kumar.

In the considered view of this court, the prosecution is also unsuccessful in establishing that the complainant has acted on the inducement made by the accused and delivered an amount of Rs.
1,09,500/- towards the purchase of the three vehicles selected by her or that the accused neither delivered the vehicles to her nor returned her money and hence, the condition as mentioned at Point no. (c) above has also not been established in the present case.
Accordingly, the accused cannot be held liable for offence u/s 420 IPC.
State Vs.: Rakesh Kumar Yadav FIR No: 453/2005 U/s 420/34 IPC P.S.Vikas Puri 19 19.

In view of the foregoing discussion, it emerges that the prosecution has miserably failed to establish beyond all reasonable doubts that accused Ajay Kumar in furtherance of common intention with his co-accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead) dishonestly induced the complainant to deliver an amount of Rs. 1,09,500/- by assuring her for delivering three second hand vehicles or that after receiving the said amount from the complainant, the accused failed to deliver the vehicles to the complainant or to return the amount paid by her.
Hence, accused deserves to be acquitted for the alleged offences.
Accordingly, accused Ajay Kumar is hereby acquitted for the offence u/s 420/34 IPC.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
To bring home the charge of common intention, prosecution has to establish by evidence, whether direct or circumstantial that there was plan or meeting of minds of all the accused persons to commit the offence for which they are charged with the aid of Section 34 IPC, be it a pre-arranged plan or plan made on the spur of moment but it must necessarily be formed before the commission State vs Rakesh Kumar Yadav on 9 April, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/145978822/
6 of crime.
Section 34 IPC does not lay down any distinct offence and rather it is a rule of evidence.
This provision also does not mandate actual commission of any overt act by any of the member of the party who has formulated the plan for committing an offence.
In the present case there is no evidence led by the prosecution to establish the existence of the common intention between accused Ajay Kumar and accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead), in furtherance of which they have allegedly cheated the complainant.
It is evident from the record that except the bald allegations to the extent the accused persons have entertained the prior criminal intention for cheating the complainant, there are no clinching evidences led by the prosecution in that regard.
More specifically, merely on the premise that the accused Ajay and co-accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav (since dead ) were related to each other as son and father respectively, it cannot be concluded that their acts were guided by the pre-arranged design to cheat the complainant.
The careful perusal of the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses would go on to reveal that there is nothing on record establishing that the accused Ajay Kumar along with his father/ co-accused Rakesh Kumar Yadav entered into prior concert or had formulated a pre- State Vs.: Rakesh Kumar Yadav FIR No: 453/2005 U/s 420/34 IPC P.S.Vikas Puri 13 arranged design for indulging into the act of cheating the complainant, hence in the considered view of this Court, the joint liability cannot be fastened upon the accused Ajay even with the aid of Section 34 IPC.
That the accused made an inducement to the complainant by way of the aforesaid misrepresentation by assuring her the delivery of the three vehicles selected by her upon payment of Rs. 1,09,500/-
c.) That the complainant acted on the inducement made by the accused and delivered an amount of Rs. 1,09,500/- towards the purchase of the three vehicles selected by her but the accused neither delivered the vehicles to her nor returned her money.
The prosecution was duty bound to establish the fact that accused Ajay Kumar was not authorized by the banks concerned for selling the bank repossessed vehicles or that the representations made by the above-named Umesh Kumar to such extent were false.
However, there is no evidence to such extent on the entire case record.
Precisely, the prosecuting agency has failed to examine the afore- named Umesh Kumar as a witness in the present case.
The presence of the witness Umesh Kumar could not be secured by the prosecuting agency for the purpose of his further examination after 27.10.2023 as he remained untraceable.
The above-named witness Umesh Kumar was a crucial witness for establishing the fact that the representation made to the complainant qua the accused persons being authorized by the banks concerned for selling the second-hand vehicles was in fact a false representation but the said witness was never completely examined in the present case.
Besides, no efforts were made by the IOs for verifying the fact of authorization of the accused persons in dealing with the repossessed bank vehicles from the banks concerned.
The fact that accused Ajay Kumar was not authorized by the banks concerned for dealing with the resale of the second hand bank repossessed vehicles has not been proved by the prosecution by any convincing evidences, hence it cannot be held that the alleged State vs Rakesh Kumar Yadav on 9 April, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/145978822/

17. Further, as the discussion in the preceding part of the judgment suggests that the prosecution has not established the alleged representation made by the accused to the complainant that he was authorized by the banks concerned for selling the second-hand vehicles was the false representation,
